column3: It repeats the son's pledge, conditioned on God's will, to be found patient and obedient to an instruction.
It frames carrying out what is revealed as a binding divine charge, though without the father-son trial.
Its "you will find me, if God wills" assurance parallels the focus's wording but concerns righteousness in a contract.
Joseph's report of a dream to his father parallels the familial setting of Abraham disclosing his vision to his son.
Abraham's prayer for a righteous child directly precedes the gift of the son tested in the focus.
The recognition of human striving loosely resonates with the son's arrival at the age of shared effort.
A reported dream seeking interpretation is only a formal parallel to Abraham's divinely significant vision.
It immediately records both father and son submitting and Abraham placing his son for the commanded act.
The possible withdrawal of revelation does not clarify the vision, command, or filial response.
The instruction to observe the recipients' response faintly parallels Abraham asking his son what he thinks.
The prophet's command to be among those who submit directly illuminates the mutual submission in the focus.
God's reaching of His command supports the certainty of the command Abraham is preparing to fulfill.
Satan's deceptive promise and battlefield retreat do not clarify the sacrificial family scene.
The announcement of a forbearing boy is the immediate antecedent to the son's appearance in the focus.
The granted respite to Iblis does not add to the father's vision or the son's obedience.
A son directing his father toward guidance provides a distant inverse of the focus's father-son exchange.
The later announcement of Isaac does not clarify the test involving the son in the focus.
Moses's determined journey to a meeting point is unrelated to the commanded sacrifice.
Solomon's failure to see the hoopoe is unrelated to Abraham's dream vision.
Belief in an earlier scripture does not clarify the focus's family trial.
It declares Abraham's vision fulfilled and explains that responsive excellence, not the son's death, confirms it.
The command to proclaim what one is ordered gives a general parallel to acting upon a divine command.
The divine call to Abraham immediately interrupts and interprets the action begun in the focus.
Revelation from God's command to warn supports divine command generally, without this particular test.
Its demonstrated restoration after death offers broad background for a vision involving sacrifice, but not its meaning.
Following ancestral tracks supplies a nearby contrast to the obedient response of Abraham and his son.
It explicitly links testing with glad tidings for the patient, clarifying the son's promised patience under trial.
Fatherly counsel that includes patience gives a close, though more general, parallel to the focus's filial exchange.
Professing submission to revealed truth loosely echoes the pair's submission in the focus.
Choosing a path to the Lord does not materially clarify the commanded family ordeal.
The river test and endurance under it provide a concrete parallel to obedience tested by divine command.
Mocking at a sign does not add to Abraham's vision or the son's reply.
Patience is named among the faithful virtues, but it adds little after the nearer trial and patience cards.
The queen's advisors ask her to consider what she commands, a structural but distant parallel to deliberation in the focus.
The universal mercy of the mission does not clarify the sacrificial test.
The unexpected gift of a son broadly parallels the miraculous granting of Abraham's requested child.
Seeking help through patience and prayer supports endurance generally, but not the specific father-son act.
It immediately names the event initiated in the focus as the clear test.
Seeing the Fire and finding no escape is an unrelated visual scene of judgment.
It explicitly counts Ishmael among the patient, directly supporting the son's pledged patience in the focus.
Deliverance from punishment in a different afterlife scene does not clarify Abraham's trial.
Its patient and grateful people offer a broad virtue parallel without the focus's testing context.
The recommendation to hire a strong, trustworthy man does not illuminate the vision or submission.
Joseph's discovery and concealment as merchandise do not clarify the focus.
The command for beautiful patience gives a useful general account of the patience the son pledges.
A son's warning to his father about punishment is a distant inverse of the focus's obedient response.
It gives the great ransom that resolves the sacrificial action prepared in the focus.
A hostile man's look during calculation does not clarify the dream or the command.
Dhu al-Qarnayn's arrival and choice of treatment are unrelated to the focus.
The polemic about daughters and sons does not add to Abraham's test of his son.
Considering food is unrelated to the father-son vision.
Jesus's announcement of a later messenger does not clarify the focus.
Reaching puberty is a distant age-stage parallel to the son's reaching the age of shared effort.
The lack of a helper for those cursed does not illuminate the focus's family trial.
Abraham's question to his father and people about worship supplies remote narrative context, not the sacrifice scene.
The preservation of Abraham's remembrance is a later honor following the ordeal begun in the focus.
It joins patience with righteous action and reward, reinforcing the faithful endurance displayed by the son.
Dhu al-Qarnayn reaching the sunrise is unrelated to the focus's reaching an age of effort.
The messenger's truthfulness and confirmation of earlier messengers do not materially clarify the family test.
The inability of false gods to create does not explain the vision or filial obedience.
Steadfast believers under hardship provide a broad parallel to patience in testing.
Idolaters confronting their alleged partners is unrelated to the focus.
The settling of every matter weakly parallels the realization of the divine command already clarified by 65:3.
The call to observe warned peoples' outcomes offers only broad nearby judgment context.
The peace bestowed on Abraham is a direct later honor within the same completed ordeal.
Moses and his companion reaching the junction do not clarify the focus.
Patience amid collective conflict is a general but less specific parallel to the son's endurance.
The adornment of the nearest heaven with stars is unrelated to the trial.
Waiting patiently for another's emergence is a distant behavioral parallel, without the commanded sacrifice.
The rescue of Noah's followers and fate of deniers gives only general consequence context.
The final surrender of idolaters is a broad contrast to the willing submission of the pair.
God's dominion and witness do not materially clarify the focus.
Pharaoh's claim to show the right way is unrelated to Abraham's true vision.
It immediately identifies Abraham's treatment as God's recompense for those who do good.
The command concerning warfare does not clarify the father-son test.
The instruction on charitable spending does not add to the focus.
The surrounding polemic over claims about God does not clarify the sacrifice narrative.
The garden owner's doubt about resurrection gives a distant contrary stance to obedience under divine disclosure.
The destruction of Pharaoh gives a general example of an evil outcome, not the focus's trial.
Zechariah's prayer for good offspring loosely parallels Abraham's earlier request already supplied by 37:100.
Household privacy rules for children do not clarify the focus.
The messenger's duty of clear delivery offers a general command-and-response framework, but not the family test.
It immediately affirms Abraham as one of God's believing servants, grounding the praise that follows his obedience.
Human formation in whatever form God wills does not clarify the focus.
The vision of wrongdoers fearing their earned consequence is a general outcome contrast to faithful obedience.
Abraham's earlier casting into the Fire provides a concrete prior trial in the same prophetic narrative.
Maintaining what God commands to be joined offers a broad command-obedience parallel only.
A son calling his father away from Satan is a distant inverse of the focus's father-led submission.
The inability to guide the spiritually blind does not clarify the focus.
Dhu al-Qarnayn reaching a barrier and meeting a people is unrelated to the focus.
Its warning that children are part of worldly adornment gives only broad background to a child becoming a test.
The differentiation of every wise matter is too general to clarify this particular command.
Household etiquette for the Prophet's home does not illuminate Abraham's vision.
Joseph's maturity and reward for excellence only loosely parallel the son's maturity and later praise of Abraham.
The number of the foremost from earlier peoples does not clarify the focus.
Denial of messengers as ordinary humans does not add to the family ordeal.
The exposure of hypocrites' hidden thoughts does not clarify the focus.
The abundance of the garden owner's produce does not add to the focus.
Patience in the face of hostile speech gives a broad but redundant parallel to the son's patience.
The argument about self-creation does not clarify Abraham's dream or the son's response.
Abraham's declaration that he is going to his Lord immediately opens the movement that leads to his prayer, son, and test.
God's testing of Abraham and his fulfillment of the tested words is the clearest general parallel to the command being carried through in the focus.
Abraham and Ishmael act together in raising the House, providing a close father-son pattern of shared obedient effort.
Abraham and Ishmael jointly pray to be made submitting to God, directly illuminating the mutual submission stated immediately after the focus.
Abraham answers God's command to submit by declaring his submission to the Lord of the worlds, directly grounding his response to the vision.
Abraham's instruction to his sons to remain in submission gives a direct paternal frame for the son's willing obedience in the focus.
Abraham's placement of his offspring in a barren valley under God gives a related picture of entrusting a son to divine purpose.
Abraham praises God for granting him Ishmael and Isaac in old age, connecting the sought son to grateful divine gift.
Ishmael is described as true to his promise and as commanding prayer and almsgiving, closely supporting the son's promised patience and obedience.
When God and His messenger decide a matter, believers have no alternative choice, directly clarifying the force of the command Abraham presents.
The faithful response to God's summons is to hear and obey, furnishing a concise parallel to the son's assent.
It explicitly calls children a test, providing direct thematic context for the son becoming the matter of Abraham's clear trial.
The sons of Adam offer sacrifices and their acceptance is distinguished, supplying another Quranic account of sacrificial offering under God.
It states that neither flesh nor blood reaches God but piety does, giving a necessary Quranic boundary for understanding sacrifice as obedient devotion.
Dedicating sacrifice, life, and death wholly to God gives a broad but direct framework for Abraham's readiness to enact the command.
The command to pray to the Lord and sacrifice is a concise ritual parallel, though it does not explain the father-son test.
